claims.claim: Samuel Harris Altman was born April 22, 1985, in Chicago; the family moved to Clayton, Missouri, in 1989. He is the eldest of four siblings (Jack, Max and Annie). His mother, Connie Gibstine, is a dermatologist; his father, Jerry Altman, was a real-estate broker.
claims.inference: Stable biographical frame. The full birth date is supported by Wikipedia (which cites Hao) and matches the existing frontmatter; Clayton and 'eldest of four' are confirmed by The New Yorker (2026).
claims.alternative: Wikipedia is tertiary; if a primary record conflicts, use the birth year only.

claims.claim: Jack Altman told The New Yorker in 2016 that Sam 'won every single game of Samurai when we were kids because he always declared himself the Samurai leader: ‘I have to win, and I’m in charge of everything.’'
claims.inference: A sibling's affectionate anecdote that shows early competitiveness and a wish to be in charge. It is consistent with the adult pattern of seeking the top role, but it is one board-game story told by a brother at a family dinner in front of a reporter.
claims.alternative: Childhood competitiveness is common to many types and to eldest siblings. The Common Reader (S05) recasts the line as Sam's general 'attitude'; quote the 2016 original with its Samurai context. The published page sources it to the Common Reader, which is secondhand.

claims.claim: The 'Mom’s Favorite' T-shirts printed for each of the four children appear only in one 2025 opinion essay (Common Reader) with no attributed source; 'restless, unceasing competition' is that essay's narration, not a Jack Altman quote.
claims.inference: Uncorroborated color. It should be cut, or attributed to the essay with its limits, not presented as fact or as Jack's words.
claims.alternative: It may come from Hagey's book or another interview not opened in this pass; a second source would allow it back in.

claims.claim: Altman received a Mac LC II for his eighth birthday in 1993 and describes it as 'this dividing line in my life: before I had a computer and after.' He fixed the family VCR at age 3 (per NYMag).
claims.inference: His own framing of technology as an identity-defining early turn. Use the exact wording 'this dividing line'.
claims.alternative: Retrospective self-mythology common in founder profiles. The published page credits the Common Reader, which does not contain it.

claims.claim: The line about 'constant (multiple times a day, I think?) affirmations of their love and belief that I could do anything' was said by Jack Altman about his own upbringing, not by Sam.
claims.inference: Correction: the published page writes 'Altman has said, his parents showered him with constant affirmations of love'. That misattributes Jack's words to Sam. It may describe the household, but not Sam's own account.
claims.alternative: Jack and Sam shared the household, so the description may apply to both, but it cannot be quoted as Sam's.

claims.claim: Altman told The New Yorker in 2016: 'Growing up gay in the Midwest in the two-thousands was not the most awesome thing. And finding AOL chat rooms was transformative. Secrets are bad when you’re eleven or twelve.'
claims.inference: Self-report of an early experience of concealment and of technology as a way to find others. It supports a story about early difference and secrecy; it does not establish a lifelong identity preoccupation.
claims.alternative: The published page says 'in the 2000s'; the source says 'in the two-thousands'. The Advocate (2024) re-quotes this; cite the New Yorker. In 2024 he told the Advocate 'I don't really think about being a gay CEO. I don’t look at it that way', and in 2026 he dismissed his sexuality's significance to his identity (C08). Both cut against reading it as the core of his self-concept.

claims.claim: At about 17, after a Christian group boycotted an assembly about sexuality at John Burroughs School, Altman addressed the school and said he was gay. He recalls being 'so nervous', 'changing the section where I told my own story back and forth like three times', and deciding: 'I’ll just tell everybody I’m gay. Whatever. Like, what’s going to happen to me?' He recalls a long standing ovation and younger students coming to him, one 'almost suicidal'. His college counsellor Madelyn Gray said: 'What Sam did changed the school.'
claims.inference: A costly, voluntary act of public self-disclosure at 17. It is the strongest early evidence that he will risk social standing to state something true about himself. It fits the published Type 4 reading (claiming difference at cost) and also a values-driven courage that any type can show.
claims.alternative: He says he was already 'mostly out' and that most people knew. The ovation and the student reactions are his own recollection two decades later; the counsellor's quote corroborates the impact. NYMag and Wikipedia describe the trigger as objections to a National Coming Out Day speaker. A single adolescent act, well received, cannot carry a lifelong motive by itself. The published page sources the counsellor quote and the boycott to Mostly Human; both are in the New Yorker 2016.

claims.claim: Altman told The New Yorker (2026) that at sixteen or seventeen he was physically attacked and subjected to homophobic slurs in St. Louis. He declined to give more detail on the record because a fuller telling would 'make me look like I’m manipulative or playing for sympathy', and he 'dismissed the idea that this event, and his sexuality broadly, was significant to his identity.' He added: 'probably that has, like, some deep-seated psychological thing—that I think I’m over but I’m not—about not wanting more conflict.'
claims.inference: Three things at once. (1) His stated reason for withholding is how the story would make him look, which is evidence of image-monitoring. (2) He minimizes the identity significance the published Type 4 thesis builds on. (3) He offers his own causal link to conflict avoidance. The causal link is his speculation, not established fact.
claims.alternative: Reticence about trauma is common and can reflect privacy or self-protection rather than image management. This is sensitive personal material reported once; use only his own words, add no detail and no causal story beyond his hedge ('probably'). Do not build a childhood-wound narrative on it.

claims.claim: His John Burroughs English teacher, Andy Abbott, recalled: 'I remember thinking—and this is an embarrassing confession—I hope he doesn’t go into technology. He’s so creative.'
claims.inference: A named teacher's recollection, via Bloomberg/Huet. It is color about early creative range, not a motive.
claims.alternative: Reported through a roundup of a paywalled Bloomberg profile that could not be checked directly.

claims.claim: Paul Graham wrote in 2008: 'Sam Altman has it. You could parachute him into an island full of cannibals and come back in 5 years and he'd be the king.' The surrounding passage names 'toughness, adaptability, determination' and Altman's 'deal-making ability'.
claims.inference: A mentor-investor's description that stresses adaptability and the ability to end up on top in any environment. That is an achievement and adaptation picture, not an inner-life one.
claims.alternative: Graham was praising a portfolio founder in a fundraising essay, so it is partly promotional. The exact wording is '5 years and he'd be the king'.

claims.claim: In 'Five Founders' (2009) Graham wrote that on 'questions of strategy or ambition I ask "What would Sama do?"' and that 'there are a few people with such force of will that they're going to get whatever they want.'
claims.inference: Graham frames Altman through ambition and will.
claims.alternative: The 'force of will' sentence is plural and general, applying to Altman only by context. The published page alters it to '[he's] going to get whatever [he] wants' and places it near a New Yorker citation; fix both.

claims.claim: Graham told The New Yorker in 2016: 'Sam is extremely good at becoming powerful.'
claims.inference: A mentor's direct characterization centered on acquiring power and position.
claims.alternative: It describes skill, not motive. An 8 seeks power to avoid being controlled; a 3 acquires it as success and status. The quote cannot separate those.

claims.claim: Altman studied computer science at Stanford for two years, dropped out and co-founded Loopt in 2005, at 19. Loopt was in Y Combinator's first batch and sold to Green Dot for $43.4 million in March 2012. In April 2012 he co-founded Hydrazine Capital with his brother Jack, using much of the roughly $5 million he received from the sale.
claims.inference: Stable career facts.
claims.alternative: Wikipedia is tertiary; the $5 million figure and the Hydrazine details should be attributed or rounded if not confirmed in a primary filing.

claims.claim: At Loopt, according to Hagey's biography as reported by The New Yorker, groups of senior employees concerned with his 'leadership and lack of transparency' asked the board on two occasions to fire him as CEO, 'But Altman inspired fierce loyalty, too.' Some employees were 'struck by his tendency to exaggerate, even about trivial things' (a Ping-Pong champion claim; Altman says he was probably joking). Mark Jacobstein, an older Loopt employee whom investors asked to act as Altman's 'babysitter', told Hagey: 'There’s a blurring between ‘I think I can maybe accomplish this thing’ and ‘I have already accomplished this thing’ that in its most toxic form leads to Theranos.'
claims.inference: This is the earliest professional evidence, from his early twenties and before OpenAI's stakes. It shows the same pattern later reported at OpenAI: an inflated presentation that blurs aspiration and accomplishment, and leadership opacity. Jacobstein's 'blurring' describes self-deception in favor of an achieving self-image, a classic Type 3 marker.
claims.alternative: Wikipedia notes Altman's supporters said the attempts 'were not serious'. Exaggeration is a common founder sales habit with a professional incentive (raising money for a pre-product startup; Emmett Shear's 'convincing phone companies to give his startup ... deals', S08). The sources are secondhand through Hagey.

claims.claim: On X in February 2023 Altman wrote: 'i failed pretty hard at my first startup–it sucked!–and am doing pretty well on my second. the thing i wish someone told me during the first one is that no one else thinks about your failures as much as you do'.
claims.inference: He frames failure as a stage on the way to success and counsels against dwelling on it. That fits a success-oriented narrative.
claims.alternative: Typical founder advice. A 4 reading treats it as failure woven into identity; nothing in the post requires that reading. Quote the lowercase original.

claims.claim: Karen Hao reports (Empire of AI, pp. 42, YC era) that after Altman became YC president he 'traded in T-shirts and cargo shorts for fitted Henleys and jeans', built muscle, 'learned to talk less, ask more questions, and project a thoughtful modesty with a furrowed brow. In private settings and with close friends, he still showed flashes of anger and frustration. In public ones and with acquaintances, he embodied the nice guy.' 'He avoided expressing negative emotions, avoided confrontation, avoided saying no to people.'
claims.inference: Hao describes a deliberate public self-presentation calibrated to what a leader should look like: the private self (anger, frustration) is managed out of the public image. This is the clearest description in the record of image construction, a Type 3 hallmark. It sits awkwardly with the Type 4 reading, which expects resistance to a manufactured persona.
claims.alternative: The book was not opened directly; the text was verified only through a critic's compilation. Hao's sources are mostly anonymous, and OpenAI declined to participate. Executive self-presentation coaching is common and can be strategic rather than motivational.

claims.claim: Graham told The New Yorker in 2016 that when he asked Altman in his kitchen, 'Do you want to take over YC?', 'he smiled, like, it worked. I had never seen an uncontrolled smile from Sam. It was like when you throw a ball of paper into the wastebasket across the room—that smile.' Altman became YC president in 2014.
claims.inference: Graham notices that the usual face is controlled and that this smile was not; what slipped through is the pleasure of a successful shot. That reads naturally as delight in a won goal (the top job) inside a usually managed presentation.
claims.alternative: One moment, read through a mentor's metaphor. The published page reads it as a 4's 'mask dropped'. It is equally a sign of a goal achieved. The original source is the 2016 article; the 2026 piece re-quotes it.

claims.claim: An unnamed 'YC stalwart' told The New Yorker in 2016: 'Sam’s a little too focussed on glory—he puts his personal brand way out front. ... Sam’s always managing up, but as the leader of the organization he needs to manage down.' Altman said of himself: 'I absolutely could do a better job at managing the organization—it was my chief weakness at Loopt'.
claims.inference: A contemporaneous insider describes attention to glory, personal brand and managing upward. Those are status- and image-oriented behaviors.
claims.alternative: Anonymous and from an organization in transition. 'Managing up' is a common critique of executives regardless of type. Altman's own reply concedes a management weakness, not a glory motive.

claims.claim: In 2016 Altman told The New Yorker that he has 'no patience for things I’m not interested in: parties, most people. When someone examines a photo and says, ‘Oh, he’s feeling this and this and this,’ all these subtle emotions, I look on with alien intrigue.' Friend's narration adds: 'His great weakness is his utter lack of interest in ineffective people'.
claims.inference: First-person evidence that he does not experience himself as attuned to subtle feeling-states. That cuts directly against a Type 4 core, which centers on emotional nuance and identification with feeling. It fits a 3 (feelings bracketed for function), and it is compatible with 5 or 8.
claims.alternative: He offers it while joking about an Asperger's suggestion, partly as self-deprecating humor. The 'ineffective people' line is the reporter's judgment, not his.

claims.claim: In January 2025 Altman told Bloomberg: 'I don’t think I’m a person with a strong EQ at all' and 'I’m not a high-EQ person.'
claims.inference: A second first-person disavowal of emotional attunement, nine years after C19. Two independent self-reports nearly a decade apart make the self-description stable. It weakens the published thesis that his identity runs on emotional depth.
claims.alternative: He says it while explaining why he missed board tension, so it doubles as an excuse; self-reported EQ is a weak measure. It also conflicts with colleagues' accounts of extraordinary attentiveness (C44), which suggests skill at reading people for influence rather than for feeling.

claims.claim: His mother, Connie Gibstine, told The New Yorker in 2016: 'Sam does keep an awful lot tied up inside. He’ll call and say he has a headache—and he’ll have Googled it ... I have to reassure him ... that it’s just stress.'
claims.inference: Family testimony that he holds stress in rather than displaying it. That is consistent with Hao's 'avoided expressing negative emotions' and his self-described anxiety (C59).
claims.alternative: A mother's affectionate aside. Holding things in fits several types (3, 5, 6) and is not specific to any.

claims.claim: Altman's statements on caring what others think conflict across time. In 2016: 'The missing circuit in my brain, the circuit that would make me care what people think about me, is a real gift.' In 2019: 'all of us, myself included, are much more affected by what other people think of us and our ideas than we like to admit' (Tyler Cowen), and 'I used to hate criticism of any sort and actively avoided it' (How To Be Successful).
claims.inference: The 2016 claim of indifference to opinion is contradicted by his own later statements and by colleagues' accounts of wanting to be liked in each interaction (C40). A self-image of not caring what people think, alongside behavior organized around approval, fits Type 3 self-deception better than a 4, who usually reports caring intensely about being seen accurately.
claims.alternative: People's self-understanding changes. The 2016 line is about risk-taking, not all approval. A Type 8 or 5 could sincerely report not caring.

claims.claim: In 'How To Be Successful' (2019) Altman writes that he wants each new project to be one 'that, if successful, will make the rest of my career look like a footnote'; that 'The most successful people I know believe in themselves almost to the point of delusion'; that 'you can bend the world to your will a surprising percentage of the time'; and that the most successful people 'are primarily internally driven; they do what they do to impress themselves'.
claims.inference: The essay is organized around outlier success, self-belief and will. The career-footnote line is a first-person statement of scale ambition. The 'internally driven' ideal can be read as his aspiration or self-image; it does not establish that he is free of the need for external validation.
claims.alternative: Advice essays describe ideals, not the author's motives. The published page reads 'impress themselves' as proof of an internal (Type 4) scoreboard; a 3 can just as easily hold this as an ideal.

claims.claim: Altman's Ozymandias remark comes from Reid Hoffman's Masters of Scale interview (YC transcript, 2018-02-23, [53:09]): the poem's image 'has been very effective in correcting bad behaviors' and 'has been an effective mental image for startup founders that got way too arrogant.'
claims.inference: A literary reference he uses instrumentally to correct founder arrogance; color more than motive.
claims.alternative: The published page credits it to Tyler Cowen, which is wrong.

claims.claim: In a 2019 Conversations with Tyler taping Altman called himself 'squarely in the good-leader, weaker-manager category'. He said of Napoleon, 'Obviously deeply flawed human, but man, impressive', admiring how 'you build a system where you can control the people' and that Napoleon 'clearly was able to use it for power'. Of his younger self: 'I was probably pretty obnoxious and a little bit of a jerk.'
claims.inference: Shows open fascination with power and systems of influence, framed as admiration with a caveat. It supports reading power and influence as central interests (3 or 8).
claims.alternative: Intellectual interest in history is not a motive. He adds 'I’m glad he does not run the United States', which distances him from the use of power.

claims.claim: In 2016 Altman told two founders at a YC party: 'I try not to think about it too much ... But I have guns, gold, potassium iodide, antibiotics, batteries, water, gas masks from the Israeli Defense Force, and a big patch of land in Big Sur I can fly to.' In 2023 he told TIME the prepper image had 'gotten caricatured very wildly' and is 'not something that I spend any serious amount of time or effort on.'
claims.inference: Shows a survival-preparedness streak that he later downplays. The later minimization is partly reputation management.
claims.alternative: Preparedness can reflect anxiety (6), self-preservation instinct in any type, or wealth-enabled hobbyism. The 2023 minimization should accompany any use of the 2016 list.

claims.claim: Altman told TIME in 2023: 'I’m a Midwestern Jew, I think that fully explains my exact mental model, very optimistic and prepared for things to go super wrong at any point.' Peter Thiel described him in 2016 as 'an optimist yet a survivalist'.
claims.inference: A self-description of optimism paired with preparedness. The optimism is a recurring self-presentation (see also 'I have never met a very successful pessimistic person', S13).
claims.alternative: A cultural self-explanation, not a motive. Optimism fits 3 and 7; preparedness fits 6.

claims.claim: Altman's 2023 compensation from OpenAI was $76,001 (tax filing). He holds no direct OpenAI equity: true after the October 2025 recapitalization and still reported in May 2026. At DealBook in December 2024 he called the job 'my childhood dream job' and said that sitting 'in the room with the smartest researchers in the world' on 'this crazy adventure' is 'worth more to me than any additional money'. In the same session he said 'if I could go back in time I would have taken it just some little bit just to never have to answer this question' and 'I wish I had taken some'. In October 2025 he wrote: 'i do wish i had taken equity a long time ago and i think it would have led to far fewer conspiracy theories'. The New Yorker (April 2026) reports he has indirect equity through a YC fund and that his stake 'could soon change'. Reuters reports a roughly $4 billion net worth from other investments.
claims.inference: The no-equity arrangement is real but weaker evidence of anti-status motivation than the published page claims. It began as a governance constraint of the nonprofit structure. He is a billionaire through other holdings. He says he wishes he had taken equity, and frames that regret around public perception ('conspiracy theories'). That last point is evidence of image-awareness.
claims.alternative: The published page's 'Meaning Over Money' bullet and its present-tense '$76,001 ... no equity ... valued at over $300 billion' are outdated or incomplete. The 'childhood dream job' line still supports a sincere mission or interest motive, which fits any type.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if OpenAI grants Altman equity, if a new Form 990 or IPO filing discloses pay, or if the S-1 becomes public.

claims.claim: Altman told The New Yorker (2026): 'This was the most fun job in the world until the day we launched ChatGPT. We were making these massive scientific discoveries' and 'since the launch of ChatGPT, the decisions have gotten very difficult'. He also said: 'of all the jobs that I think I could reasonably do, this is the most stressful one I can imagine.' In Reflections (Jan 2025) he called the years 'the most rewarding, fun, best, interesting, exhausting, stressful, and—particularly for the last two—unpleasant years of my life so far.'
claims.inference: He prefers the discovery phase to the public-facing, high-stakes phase. That is a common founder sentiment and does not discriminate between types.
claims.alternative: The published page reads this as a 4's 'wound' (meaning curdles when it meets the world). An equally plausible reading is ordinary preference for building over managing scrutiny.

claims.claim: Altman told The New Yorker (2026): 'I’m very ambitious as far as, like, my hope for humanity, and what I expect us all to achieve. I weirdly have very little personal ambition.' He then added: 'No one believes you’re doing this just because it’s interesting ... You’re doing it for power or for some other thing.'
claims.inference: A disavowal of personal ambition sits against Graham's 'extremely good at becoming powerful' (C12), his own career-footnote goal (C23) and most New Yorker sources' 'relentless will to power' (C40). A sincere-seeming denial of personal ambition alongside a sustained climb to the top fits Type 3 self-deception, where the achieving self is identified with the mission.
claims.alternative: He may mean it. His professed motives (technology is 'cool', influence over its direction, C28) could be honest and not status-driven. The authors note even people close to him cannot tell where 'hope for humanity' ends and ambition begins.

claims.claim: A former OpenAI employee told The New Yorker (2026) that Altman once said: 'I don’t care about money. I care more about power.'
claims.inference: If accurate, it reframes the no-equity story: money is not the currency, power is. That supports power/status drives (3 or 8) over the meaning-only reading.
claims.alternative: Anonymous recollection of an informal remark, not on the record. Altman says he is not primarily motivated by wealth. Use only with attribution to 'a former employee recalled', or omit.

claims.claim: On November 17, 2023, the OpenAI board fired Altman on a Google Meet call while he was in Las Vegas for the Formula 1 Grand Prix. The board said he 'was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities' and 'The board no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI.'
claims.inference: The documented event that anchors the firing section.
claims.alternative: The board's statement gave no specifics. WilmerHale later found the board acted within its discretion but that his conduct 'did not mandate removal' (C50).

claims.claim: That evening Altman posted 'i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit.' Hours later he posted: 'i love you all. today was a weird experience in many ways. but one unexpected one is that it has been sorta like reading your own eulogy while you’re still alive. the outpouring of love is awesome. one takeaway: go tell your friends how great you think they are.'
claims.inference: His public response reframes rejection as an outpouring of love, a positive public face within hours. It shows reception-focused framing: how others see him is the experience he reports.
claims.alternative: Gratitude in the moment is also a genuine human response, and a strategic one: the public campaign for his return began that night (S43). Quote the lowercase originals in full.

claims.claim: Within days, 745 of OpenAI's 770 employees signed a letter threatening to resign unless the board resigned. Altman's return was agreed November 21-22, 2023. Under the deal Altman and Brockman did not retake board seats; Altman rejoined the board in March 2024 after the WilmerHale review.
claims.inference: Documented. The employee rally shows deep loyalty among staff, a real counterweight to the critics' testimony.
claims.alternative: Employees also had financial stakes (a pending tender at an $86 billion valuation, S43) and a Microsoft exit option, so the letter mixes loyalty with incentives.

claims.claim: Greg Brockman, removed from the board the same day, posted his message to staff: 'but based on today’s news, i quit.' He returned with Altman, took a sabbatical announced August 5, 2024 ('First time to relax since co-founding OpenAI 9 years ago') and returned November 12, 2024.
claims.inference: Documented loyalty from the closest co-founder.
claims.alternative: The published page's 'Based on today's news, I quit' should be quoted in lowercase starting from 'but'. 'relax and recharge' is not Brockman's wording.

claims.claim: On Lex Fridman's podcast (March 2024) Altman called the firing 'definitely the most painful professional experience of my life, and chaotic and shameful and upsetting and a bunch of other negative things.' He described 'this fugue state for the month after, maybe 45 days after', said 'the dominant emotion of the weekend was love, not hate', and said: 'I think I’m like an extremely trusting person'.
claims.inference: He names shame among several negative feelings. The published page's central 'shameful' argument rests on this one word, but it is a single adjective in a run-on list, not a chosen standalone word. It cannot discriminate Type 4 from Type 3: shame is the heart-triad emotion for 2, 3 and 4, and public firing triggers it in most people.
claims.alternative: The published page renders it as 'Chaotic. And shameful. And upsetting.' and builds a section on 'the word that stayed'. Quote the clause as spoken.

claims.claim: In January 2025 Altman told Bloomberg that when board members first called about his return he was 'initially just supermad and said no' and demanded 'Only if the whole board quits'; when the board named Emmett Shear CEO he thought 'All right, now I’m f---ing really done,' because 'that was real deception.' Asked if he was traumatized, he said 'I totally was' and that 'all those people that I feel like really f---ed me and f---ed the company were gone, and now I had to clean up their mess', walking his house at night 'f---ing depressed and tired. And it felt so unfair.' He also said 'they were not happy with the way that I tried to get them off the board. Lesson learned on that.'
claims.inference: He reports anger, a sense of injustice and a hard power demand (the whole board must go). That cuts against the published page's TL;DR claim that he 'didn't call it unfair or political', and shows that he does fight hard when his position is threatened. The anger is reported retrospectively, in a controlled interview.
claims.alternative: It supports the 8 alternative (a demand for control under attack) and ordinary anger at a firing. The New Yorker reports similar language ('Absolutely fucking not', C38).

claims.claim: The New Yorker (2026) reports that Altman ran a 'sort of government-in-exile' from his San Francisco house with advisers including Ron Conway, Brian Chesky and Chris Lehane, who built a public case for his return. He interrupted the war room at six each evening with Negronis ('You need to chill'). He recalled thinking 'Absolutely fucking not' about returning under suspicion, and described the aftermath as 'just this weird fugue.'
claims.inference: The response to threat was organized, image-focused and campaign-like: crisis communications, a public narrative, allies working the press. That reads as 3-like competence under threat as much as any 4 dissociation.
claims.alternative: The published page reads 'weird fugue' and 'eulogy' as Type 4 dissociation metaphors. Shock language after a sudden firing is common and does not discriminate types. Lex Fridman's account (C36) places the fugue in the weeks after the return.

claims.claim: On a tense call the day he was fired, as the board pressed him to acknowledge a pattern of deception, Altman said 'This is just so fucked up' repeatedly and also 'I can’t change my personality', according to people on the call. Altman says he does not recall the exchange and that 'It’s possible I meant something like ‘I do try to be a unifying force,’' attributing the criticism to a tendency, especially early in his career, 'to be too much of a conflict avoider'. A board member said: 'What it meant was ‘I have this trait where I lie to people, and I’m not going to stop.’'
claims.inference: Whatever he meant, his own gloss links the trait to unifying people and avoiding conflict, not to an inner identity. That is evidence for accommodation, not Type 4 self-definition.
claims.alternative: Contested on every side: anonymous recall, his non-recollection, opposing interpretations. The published page says he 'said the same thing over and over'; only 'This is just so fucked up' is described as repeated. It calls the line 'the purest Type 4 statement in the archive', but it supports no single type.

claims.claim: The New Yorker (Farrow and Marantz, April 2026, 100+ interviews) wrote that 'most of the people we spoke to shared the judgment of Sutskever and Amodei: Altman has a relentless will to power'. An unnamed board member said: 'He’s unconstrained by truth ... He has two traits that are almost never seen in the same person. The first is a strong desire to please people, to be liked in any given interaction. The second is almost a sociopathic lack of concern for the consequences that may come from deceiving someone.' The authors wrote: 'His greatest strength has always been his ability to convince disparate groups that what he wants and what they need are one and the same.'
claims.inference: The board member's first trait, 'a strong desire to please people, to be liked in any given interaction', is a close lay description of the Type 3 pattern of shaping the presented self to what wins approval in each room. Joined to a sustained will to power and to deception, it is also the core of the critics' case.
claims.alternative: An anonymous, adversarial characterization by someone involved in the firing. 'Sociopathic' is a pejorative, not a diagnosis, and must not be repeated as one. 'Relentless will to power' is the authors' synthesis, not a direct source quote. Altman called the article 'incendiary' (C72). A desire to be liked also fits Types 2 and 9.

claims.claim: In an April 10, 2026 blog post Altman wrote: 'I am not proud of being conflict-averse, which has caused great pain for me and OpenAI. I am not proud of handling myself badly in a conflict with our previous board that led to a huge mess for the company.' He added: 'I am sorry to people I’ve hurt and wish I had learned more faster.' He also wrote that he is proud of how he 'held the line on not being willing to agree to the unilateral control' Musk wanted. He told The New Yorker his main flaw as a manager had been 'his eagerness to avoid conflict' and that 'Now I’m very happy to fire people quickly'.
claims.inference: His own repeated admission that conflict avoidance is a core, costly flaw. Together with C08 and C39, Altman himself names accommodation-to-avoid-conflict, not identity or feeling, as his defining weakness. That is strong first-person evidence against Type 8, which confronts, and it matches the colleague testimony (C42-C46).
claims.alternative: Conflict avoidance is central to Type 9 and common in 2 and 3. Holding the line against Musk shows he can refuse a powerful counterpart when control is at stake, which keeps 8 in view. The post was written under acute stress after an attack on his home.

claims.claim: Keach Hagey, author of the biography 'The Optimist' (2025), who interviewed Altman several times, said: 'he is not great at dealing with conflict, so he’ll basically tell people what they want to hear. That causes a lot of sturm und drang in the management ranks, and it’s a pattern.' She said it happened at Loopt, where executives asked the board to replace him, and at OpenAI. Of his trust problems: 'This happened both at his first startup and very famously at OpenAI, as well as at Y Combinator.' She calls him 'a salesman' who is 'really excellent at getting in a room and convincing people that he can see the future and that he has something in common with them.'
claims.inference: A biographer with direct access names one pattern across three organizations and two decades: telling people what they want to hear to avoid conflict. Repetition across contexts and time is what the standard asks for. It favors an approval-adaptive motive (3, or 9/2) over a 4 who protects emotional authenticity.
claims.alternative: Hagey explicitly offers the incentive explanation: 'a typical critique of people who have the salesman skill set'. A fundraiser-CEO's job rewards telling each audience what it wants. The pattern could be learned practice rather than core motive, although it predates OpenAI's stakes.

claims.claim: Karen Hao reports that 'Many of Altman’s closest executives had long observed a particular pattern in his behavior: If two teams disagreed, he often agreed in private with each of their perspectives, which created confusion and bred mistrust among colleagues.' In her book she describes him expressing sympathy to the Safety team while pressing the Applied team to keep going.
claims.inference: A concrete behavioral form of telling each party what it wants: agreement mirrors whoever is in the room. Supports C42.
claims.alternative: Anonymous sources. A CEO keeping factions on board may be deliberate management, not a need for approval. 'Telling people what they want to hear' does not appear literally in the Atlantic excerpt.

claims.claim: A colleague who worked with him for several years at Loopt told Hao: 'Sam remembers all these details about you. He’s so attentive. But then part of it is he uses that to figure out how to influence you in different ways. He’s so good at adjusting to what you say, and you really feel like you’re making progress with him. And then you realize over time that you’re actually just running in place.' Hao writes that he 'sometimes lied about details so insignificant that it was hard to say why the dishonesty mattered at all', which one person called 'paper cuts'.
claims.inference: Describes adaptive mirroring ('adjusting to what you say') and attentiveness used for influence, at Loopt, years before OpenAI. Cross-time support for the pattern in C42 and C43.
claims.alternative: Verified only via a critic's compilation of the book; anonymous. The published page presents these as general OpenAI-era observations; they concern the Loopt years. Attentive listening also fits Type 2.

claims.claim: In the 'Honest Thoughts' email of September 20, 2017, Ilya Sutskever (signing for himself and Greg Brockman) wrote to Altman: 'We don't understand why the CEO title is so important to you. Your stated reasons have changed, and it's hard to really understand what's driving it.' In the same email they praised Altman as 'a genuine counterbalance' to Musk: 'Sam stood his ground'.
claims.inference: Contemporaneous co-founders, six years before the firing, puzzled that the top title mattered so much and that his stated reasons shifted. Title importance plus shifting rationales fits a status-oriented self that adapts its explanations. The same email credits him with firmness against Musk, which complicates a pure conflict-avoider picture.
claims.alternative: Written during a high-stakes negotiation over control; co-founders had their own interests. Litigation release via a third-party compilation; court PDF not opened.

claims.claim: Sutskever's 2023 memos to the board included a list headed 'Sam exhibits a consistent pattern of . . .' whose first item is 'Lying'. In one memo he worried about entrusting AI to someone who 'just tells people what they want to hear.' In a 2025 deposition Sutskever said much of the material came from Mira Murati and 'I knew it through secondhand knowledge.' Murati told The New Yorker: 'Everything I shared was accurate, and I stand behind all of it.'
claims.inference: Another independent use of 'tells people what they want to hear' (2023), by a co-founder.
claims.alternative: Secondhand and contested; the memo itself was not produced. Murati stands by her account; Sutskever regretted the rushed process. Do not present 'consistent pattern of lying' as established.

claims.claim: Helen Toner said on the TED AI Show (May 28, 2024) that 'for years, Sam had made it really difficult for the board to actually do that job by, you know, withholding information. Misrepresenting things that were happening at the company, in some cases outright lying to the board.' She said 'We learned about ChatGPT on Twitter', that he did not disclose owning the OpenAI Startup Fund, that 'On multiple occasions, he gave us inaccurate information about the small number of. Formal safety processes', and that 'after the paper came out, Sam started lying to other board members in order to try and push me off the board.' Board chair Bret Taylor responded that OpenAI was 'disappointed that Ms. Toner continues to revisit these issues.' Altman told Bloomberg in January 2025 he has 'a different memory and interpretation' about ChatGPT and said 'I don’t think I was doing things that were sneaky', explaining the Startup Fund ownership as a structural necessity.
claims.inference: First-person testimony from a board member who voted to fire him. It is consistent in kind with C41-C46: managing information and others' impressions to keep control without open conflict.
claims.alternative: Toner is an interested party. OpenAI and WilmerHale dispute the framing. Quote Toner from the TED transcript (Fortune's wording differs). Attribute and give responses.

claims.claim: The Washington Post (Dec 8, 2023) reported, citing two unnamed people, that senior employees described Altman as 'psychologically abusive, creating chaos at the artificial-intelligence start-up', including allegedly 'pitting employees against each other in unhealthy ways', and that these complaints were a major factor in the firing. The Post also reported that board members 'didn’t use the language of abuse' themselves. Toner said two executives 'used the phrase psychological abuse'. OpenAI's spokesperson and executive Anna Makanju disputed the characterization.
claims.inference: Serious allegations relevant to the shadow side of influence-seeking. Their type relevance is limited.
claims.alternative: Anonymous, secondhand and paraphrased: none of the WaPo phrases is a quotation. Executives later minimized what they said, per Toner. A sensitive allegation; attribute precisely and include rebuttals. The published page's 'Two executives used the phrase psychological abuse' should credit Toner, not the Post.

claims.claim: Bloomberg reported (December 2023, unnamed sources) that in lobbying for Helen Toner's removal Altman misrepresented other directors' views, including telling some that Tasha McCauley had said 'Helen's obviously got to go', a characterization McCauley resisted. It also reported that he offered to apologize publicly for misrepresenting views and that, in return negotiations, he 'pushed for a statement from the board absolving him of wrongdoing.' OpenAI said the account 'significantly differs from Sam's recollection.' In March 2024 Altman apologized for believing that 'a former OpenAI board member was harming OpenAI through their actions'.
claims.inference: Seeking a public absolution statement as a condition of return is evidence of concern for his public record and image under threat. Altman's own 'Lesson learned on that' (C37) acknowledges the board-removal effort.
claims.alternative: Anonymous sourcing, disputed by OpenAI. Seeking exoneration is also a rational legal and reputational move for any CEO.

claims.claim: OpenAI's summary of the WilmerHale review (March 8, 2024) said WilmerHale 'found there was a breakdown in trust between the prior Board and Mr. Altman', that the decision 'did not arise out of concerns regarding product safety or security, the pace of development, OpenAI’s finances, or its statements to investors, customers, or business partners', and that the board 'acted within its broad discretion' but 'his conduct did not mandate removal.' No written report was released.
claims.inference: Documented outcome: neither exoneration of the candor concerns nor a finding that removal was required.
claims.alternative: Written by the post-reinstatement board; the New Yorker reports the findings were oral briefings only.

claims.claim: In an email to Elon Musk on February 18, 2023 Altman wrote: 'well, you’re my hero and that’s what it feels like when you attack openai. i am tremendously thankful for everything you’ve done to help–i don’t think openai would have happened without you–and it really fucking hurts when you publicly attack openai.' Musk replied that it was 'certainly not my intention to be hurtful'.
claims.inference: A private, direct expression of hurt to an adversary. It is the strongest evidence that he does voice feeling in conflict, and it supports the published Type 4 reading's 'vulnerability first'. It is also a relational appeal (a 2-like move) that seeks to repair the relationship by naming admiration and hurt.
claims.alternative: Written privately to a powerful co-founder and funder whose attacks threatened OpenAI; it may be strategic as well as sincere. It was an email, not a text, and is all lowercase.

claims.claim: In December 2024 Altman told Bari Weiss that Musk 'did a lot to help OpenAI in the early days' and is 'a sort of legendary entrepreneur', and also 'He's also clearly a bully, and he's also someone who clearly likes to get in fights. Right now it's me. It's been Bezos, Gates, Zuckerberg, lots of other people'. At DealBook the same month he said: 'This is tremendously sad. I grew up with Elon as like a mega hero ... I have different feelings about him now, but I'm still glad he exists.'
claims.inference: He pairs criticism with praise and depersonalizes the conflict as a pattern in Musk. This is a measured public posture that keeps him likeable and makes Musk the aggressor.
claims.alternative: Quote the audio: 'with Elon as like a mega hero' and 'I'm still glad he exists'. Both readings remain: genuine ambivalence (published 4 reading) or a well-managed public image (3).

claims.claim: When Musk led a $97.4 billion bid for OpenAI's controlling nonprofit, Altman posted 'no thank you but we will buy twitter for $9.74 billion if you want' (Feb 10, 2025). He told Bloomberg TV: 'Probably his whole life is from a position of insecurity, I feel for the guy' and 'I don’t think he’s, like, a happy person ... I feel for him.'
claims.inference: Public jabs delivered as wit and pity. He wins the exchange without appearing aggressive.
claims.alternative: The published page reads the 'insecurity' remark as empathy. It can equally be a status move that frames the rival as pitiable. Use the corrected wording.

claims.claim: In 2016 Altman wrote that Trump 'is irresponsible in the way dictators are', that 'To anyone familiar with the history of Germany in the 1930s, it's chilling to watch Trump in action', and that 'Donald Trump represents an unprecedented threat to America'. ABC reports a March 2017 tweet: 'I think Trump is terrible and few things would make me happier than him not being president.' In December 2024 he gave $1 million to Trump's inaugural fund ('He’s the president of the United States. I support any president.'). On January 21, 2025 he said at the Stargate announcement: 'We wouldn’t be able to do this without you, Mr. President'. On January 22 he posted: 'watching @potus more carefully recently has really changed my perspective on him (i wish i had done more of my own thinking and definitely fell in the npc trap).'
claims.inference: A documented reversal tied to business interests, recast as personal growth and independent thinking ('npc trap'). Adapting the stance to the audience in power, then presenting the change as authenticity, fits Type 3 image adaptation. The published page reads it as a 4's horror of being ordinary.
claims.alternative: Many executives courted the new administration for corporate reasons; this may be pure business pragmatism rather than a type motive. The March 2017 tweet rests on ABC only. The published page says he 'posted on X' in 2016; it was a 2017 tweet.

claims.claim: In 'Reflections' (January 2025) Altman wrote: 'Our vision won’t change; our tactics will continue to evolve.' He told The New Yorker (2026) that some people want a leader who 'is going to be absolutely sure of what they think and stick with it, and it’s not going to change. And we are in a field, in an area, where things change extremely quickly.' His April 2026 post lists 'Adaptability is critical' among his beliefs.
claims.inference: He makes a principle of flexibility in stated positions, which is consistent with an adaptive self-presentation.
claims.alternative: Strategic flexibility is sensible in a fast-moving field and is not a personality motive in itself.

claims.claim: At TED2025, pressed on trust and power, Altman said: 'Look, I think like anyone else, I’m a nuanced character that doesn’t reduce well to one dimension here. So, you know, probably some of the good things are true and probably some of the criticism is true.' Shown a 'Ring of Power' image, he answered with a question: 'How do you think I’m doing relative to other CEOs that have gotten a lot of power ...?'
claims.inference: A deflection that manages the impression under hostile questioning: he concedes in general and contests in particular.
claims.alternative: The published page reads 'nuanced character' as 4-style self-narration. It is equally standard media handling. Cite the transcript, not VentureBeat.

claims.claim: Former OpenAI board member Sue Yoon told The New Yorker (2026) that Altman was 'not this Machiavellian villain' but able, to the point of 'fecklessness', to convince himself of the shifting realities of his sales pitches: 'He’s too caught up in his own self-belief. So he does things that, if you live in the real world, make no sense. But he doesn’t live in the real world.'
claims.inference: A named, relatively sympathetic insider describes self-deception: he believes his own pitch. That is the Type 3 passion (deceit as identification with the image) more precisely than lying, and it matches Jacobstein's 'blurring' at Loopt (C14).
claims.alternative: Named but brief. The published page claims Yoon 'ended up describing a Type 4'; nothing in her words is specific to 4.

claims.claim: Altman wrote in 2019 that 'Self-belief must be balanced with self-awareness. I used to hate criticism of any sort and actively avoided it.' In Reflections (2025) he called the firing 'a big failure of governance by well-meaning people, myself included' and said 'I’d like to believe I’m a better, more thoughtful leader today'.
claims.inference: Consistent self-presentation as someone on a growth arc. It acknowledges faults in general terms while leaving specific allegations unaddressed (see C47).
claims.alternative: Public self-improvement narratives are common among executives.

claims.claim: In a January 2022 Art of Accomplishment episode Altman said: 'I think I started off my career in life as a very anxious, high-strung person, much more than I realized' and 'every day I would come to work in some sort of a panic. I would think we were doing the wrong things.' He described unstructured meditation, 'sitting for an hour with your eyes closed and making no effort towards anything', and 'this very deep-felt sense that there is no self that I can still find to identify with in any way at all.'
claims.inference: He reports anxiety behind a calm exterior and a meditation-derived sense of no fixed self. The anxiety fits 6 and is common in 3s whose worth depends on performance. The no-self insight is a contemplative report, not type evidence.
claims.alternative: The published page's 'I would wake up in the middle of the night with my heart pounding, just terrified' is unsourced (only in an anonymous Medium compilation, S99) and must be removed. Use 'no self that I can still find to identify with'. 'Crippling Anxiety' is the episode title, not his words.

claims.claim: On the Relentless podcast (July 2026) Altman said, crediting Naval Ravikant, that 'the opposite of a bad experience is no experience', that with a fast-forward button on your life 'your life would be over', that the boring and bad parts are 'all part of the like interestingness of and the kind of like emotional depth and range', and 'I find it like fairly easy to be grateful for the bad days.'
claims.inference: A philosophy of valuing all experience, including bad experience. The published page treats it as the clearest Type 4 statement ('emotional depth and range'). It is borrowed from Naval, framed as founder advice, and reframes pain as interesting. That is also compatible with 7-style reframing and with a meditator's equanimity.
claims.alternative: Auto-captions only. The published page cleans the quote and removes 'like'. One podcast answer from 2026 cannot carry the type alone, especially against his repeated low-EQ self-description (C19, C20).

claims.claim: In 2016 Altman told The New Yorker: 'I’m on Team Human. I don’t have a good logical reason why I’m sad, except that the class of things that humans are better at continues to narrow.' After a moment: '‘Melancholy’ is a better word than ‘sad.’'
claims.inference: His own choice of 'melancholy' about humanity's narrowing advantage is a 4-flavored word. It is the best single piece of support for a 4 or 4-wing coloring in his vocabulary.
claims.alternative: It concerns AI's trajectory, not his self. It is one remark.

claims.claim: On February 2, 2026 Altman posted that after building an app with Codex, 'at least a couple of' its feature ideas 'were better than I was thinking of. I felt a little useless and it was sad.' He added: 'I am sure we will figure out much better and more interesting ways to spend our time, and amazing new ways to be useful to each other, but I am feeling nostalgic for the present.'
claims.inference: He names sadness at being outperformed, and at losing usefulness and competence. Feeling useless when no longer the best contributor fits a 3's worth-through-performance as well as a 4's wistfulness ('nostalgic for the present').
claims.alternative: He frames it as going 'off-script', a self-aware public post by the CEO selling the tool, so it doubles as marketing. Quote the post, not Fortune's altered version.

claims.claim: Altman married Oliver Mulherin (they met in 2015) in a small ceremony; Wikipedia places it in January 2024 at their Hawaii estate. NBC reported it on January 11, 2024. Their son was born in February 2025 ('i have never felt such love'). He told Bloomberg in June 2025: 'I remember in like the first hour I like felt this neurochemical change ... Like I am being like neuro chemically hacked. But I'm like noticing it happening' and that fatherhood 'totally rewired all of my priorities.' Fortune reported in June 2026 that the couple are expecting another child later in 2026.
claims.inference: Warmth and an observing stance toward his own feeling ('noticing it happening'). A personal counterweight to the critical sections.
claims.alternative: The exact wedding date and place rest on Wikipedia (PinkNews says late 2023). A second child is reported as expected, not born. Quote the lowercase birth post and the Bloomberg captions, or attribute Fortune's cleaned version.
claims.review_trigger: Update when a second child's birth is publicly confirmed.

claims.claim: At the May 16, 2023 Senate Judiciary hearing Altman said: 'My worst fears are that we cause significant--we, the field, the technology, the industry cause significant harm to the world.' The line 'You should be skeptical of any company calling for its own regulation', which the published page attributes to him there, is not in the official record.
claims.inference: Documented testimony. The fabricated or misattributed 'skeptical' line must be removed, along with the paragraph that interprets it as 'the compulsion ... to be honest about your own contradictions'.
claims.alternative: None; the official GPO record is authoritative.

claims.claim: OpenAI created a 'capped-profit' LP in March 2019, with first-round investor returns capped at 100x. The announcement, by Brockman and Sutskever, said 'no pre-existing legal structure we know of strikes the right balance'. In May 2025 Altman wrote that the capped-profit structure 'made sense when it looked like there might be one dominant AGI effort but doesn’t in a world of many great AGI companies'. In October 2025 OpenAI recapitalized as a public benefit corporation (OpenAI Group), with the OpenAI Foundation holding 26%. Its mission statement changed from building AI that 'safely benefits humanity' to 'ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity.' The quote 'We needed a structure that didn't exist' was not found in any source.
claims.inference: Documented structural arc: a novel safeguard was invented, then abandoned when it constrained growth. That is consistent with tactics evolving in service of winning.
claims.alternative: Many stakeholders shaped these decisions (investors, attorneys general, Microsoft). The published page's Altman quote 'We needed a structure that didn't exist' must be removed or replaced with S32 (not his words) or S33 (his).

claims.claim: In May 2024 Ilya Sutskever left OpenAI, and Jan Leike resigned, posting: 'But over the past years, safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products.' OpenAI disbanded its Superalignment team, which a year earlier it had promised 20% of its computing power over four years. In April 2025 Geoffrey Hinton said: 'I would like them to execute that mission instead of enriching their investors.'
claims.inference: Documented criticism from inside and outside OpenAI about the safety-versus-product trade-off under Altman.
claims.alternative: Organizational outcomes have many authors. Hinton's quote comes from CNBC, not the TIME article the published page links. Leike's post ID in the published page is wrong.

claims.claim: In September 2026 Altman told Fortune: 'given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that' and 'I would say not 2026.' On X he wrote: 'I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier' and 'Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same.' On September 29 he said he has no 'particular timeline in mind' for an IPO and 'this is a time to put safety and mission first.' OpenAI had announced on June 8, 2026 that it 'recently submitted a confidential S-1'. In December 2025 he said he was '0%' excited to be a public-company CEO.
claims.inference: A safety-forward public turn alongside a filed IPO path. It can be read as a sincere recalibration, as Type 3 timing of the market around a bad safety news cycle, or as both. The record cannot yet separate those readings; whether evaluators are actually embedded at OpenAI is the test.
claims.alternative: The published page attributes the safety quote to Fox Business with 'that's happening' and an ellipsis; prefer Fortune's wording. Use '0%', not 'Zero percent'.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check when OpenAI announces embedded independent evaluators, files a public S-1, or sets an IPO date.

claims.claim: World (originally Worldcoin), co-founded by Altman, scans irises with a device to verify unique humans. MIT Technology Review's 2022 investigation subheadline said it had so far built 'a biometric database from the bodies of the poor'. Kenya suspended Worldcoin enrollment on August 2, 2023.
claims.inference: Documented facts about a venture he co-founded. The published page reads it as an identity-obsessed project; it equally fits ambition for global scale.
claims.alternative: The MIT TR line is the magazine's own subheadline, not a critic's quote. Altman was not interviewed for that piece. Founding year and current status should be checked if used.

claims.claim: Altman's sister Annie has publicly alleged since at least November 2021 that he sexually abused her in childhood. In January 2025 she filed a federal lawsuit in the Eastern District of Missouri. Sam, their mother Connie and brothers Max and Jack issued a statement: 'All of these claims are utterly untrue. This situation causes immense pain to our entire family.' On March 20, 2026 the court dismissed her common-law claims as time-barred with leave to amend. She filed an amended complaint on April 1, 2026 under a Missouri statute for childhood sexual abuse claims. Sam is countersuing for defamation. As of September 30, 2026 the case was active (discovery due October 23, 2026; dispositive motions due November 16, 2026; a hearing set for October 2, 2026). A December 2025 order set a jury trial for May 3, 2027. The New Yorker 'could not substantiate Annie’s account.'
claims.inference: A grave, unresolved allegation that a responsible profile must acknowledge, with the denial and its unresolved status. It is not type evidence and must not be used to support or undermine any type argument.
claims.alternative: Unadjudicated, contested, and involving mental-health characterizations in the family statement that should not be repeated as fact. The published page's 'The litigation is ongoing' remains accurate as of 2026-09-30, but the procedural posture has changed. Keep medical and IME details out of copy.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check the docket (courtlistener 69520118) after the Oct 2, 2026 hearing, the Nov 16, 2026 dispositive-motion deadline, and the May 3, 2027 trial date; update immediately on dismissal, settlement or verdict.

claims.claim: In the Musk v. OpenAI trial Altman testified on May 12, 2026. Asked 'Do you always tell the truth?', he answered 'I believe I’m a truthful person', then 'I’m sure there is some time in my life when I have not' (per The Ringer), and said 'I believe I am an honest and trustworthy businessperson.' Of the 2023 firing he testified that he was 'completely caught off guard' and that he was upset, angry and hurt. On May 18, 2026 a unanimous jury found Musk had waited too long to sue; Musk's lawyers said they would appeal.
claims.inference: Sworn testimony on his honesty under adversarial questioning. Useful as a dated anchor for the trust question.
claims.alternative: NPR renders one answer as 'some times in my life when I did not'; name the outlet. A remark that Musk 'did try to kill it' was struck from the record.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if Musk's appeal is filed or decided.

claims.claim: On April 10, 2026 a man threw a Molotov cocktail at Altman's San Francisco home and a 20-year-old suspect was arrested; no one was hurt. That night Altman posted a family photo 'in the hopes that it might dissuade the next person', called the New Yorker investigation 'an incendiary article', and wrote: 'Now I am awake in the middle of the night and pissed, and thinking that I have underestimated the power of words and narratives.'
claims.inference: A dated event and his raw response. His framing centers on 'words and narratives', a sign of how central the public story is to him.
claims.alternative: A frightening attack; anger and narrative-blame are ordinary responses under threat. Do not publish address details.

claims.claim: Altman's April 2026 post called the New Yorker investigation 'an incendiary article'. Ronan Farrow said the story 'was meticulously fact-checked, and OpenAI is not disputing the core facts.'
claims.inference: Context for weighing the New Yorker's testimony: Altman rejects its framing, and its author says its core facts are not disputed.
claims.alternative: Both statements are self-interested.

claims.claim: 'Artificial', Luca Guadagnino's biographical comedy-drama about Altman's 2023 firing and rehiring, starring Andrew Garfield as Altman with a screenplay by Simon Rich, has its world premiere at the New York Film Festival on October 5, 2026 (Alice Tully Hall). Neon releases it in U.S. theaters on December 25, 2026. On September 29, 2026 Altman said of its trailer: 'looks like an awful movie, but I appreciate people’s creativity, and I really do support that' and that if people need to 'poke fun at me, it doesn’t bother me.' The film is a dramatization and is not evidence about his psychology.
claims.inference: Current context that explains renewed search interest. His comment is a light, likeable public posture toward ridicule.
claims.alternative: Release details may change (limited vs wide release is unconfirmed). Reviews and the film's accuracy are unknown as of 2026-10-05. The published page's line that he cannot rule this 'island' is speculative; he has now commented publicly.
claims.review_trigger: After NYFF reviews and the Dec 25, 2026 release, re-check reception and any further Altman comment; never cite the film as evidence of motive.

claims.claim: Altman has been OpenAI's CEO since 2019 (briefly removed in November 2023) and still held the title as of October 4, 2026.
claims.inference: Current-role check.
claims.alternative: None.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check on any leadership change or IPO.

claims.claim: Across three organizations and two decades, independent sources describe one recurring behavior: Altman accommodates the person or faction in front of him to avoid conflict and keep approval, by telling people what they want to hear, agreeing privately with each side, adjusting to what you say, and avoiding saying no. They include Loopt colleagues (2000s, via Hao and Hagey), YC observers (2014-2019, via Hao and Hagey), co-founders in 2017 ('Your stated reasons have changed'), board members and executives in 2023 ('just tells people what they want to hear'; 'a strong desire to please people, to be liked in any given interaction'), and his biographer in 2025. Altman independently names the same trait as his defining flaw: 'too much of a conflict avoider' (2026), 'I am not proud of being conflict-averse, which has caused great pain' (April 2026), and a 'deep-seated psychological thing ... about not wanting more conflict' (2026).
claims.inference: This is the strongest repeated, costly, cross-context pattern in the record, and he acknowledges it himself. It cost him a near-ouster at Loopt, the 2023 firing, and years of trust problems. The motive it best fits is keeping a winning, approved image in each interaction while pursuing the goal: Type 3's adaptation of the presented self. A core 4 typically protects an authentic self-expression even at the cost of approval. The pattern also argues against 8, who confronts.
claims.alternative: Professional incentive is the main rival explanation: a fundraiser-salesman CEO is paid to tell each audience what it wants (Hagey's own caveat). Much of the testimony is anonymous or adversarial. Type 9 (conflict avoidance, merging) and Type 2 (wanting to be liked, attentiveness) also explain the accommodation; the ambition and power drive (C76) separates 3 from 9, and the achievement focus separates 3 from 2. The single loud counterexample is the private 2023 email to Musk naming hurt (C51).

claims.claim: Ambition and power are consistent through the record. Jack's childhood 'I have to win, and I’m in charge of everything' (2016). Graham's 'extremely good at becoming powerful' (2016) and his 'force of will' framing (2009). His own wish for each project to make 'the rest of my career look like a footnote' (2019). His 'bend the world to your will' (2019). Co-founders' puzzlement at 'why the CEO title is so important to you' (2017). Most New Yorker sources' 'relentless will to power' (2026). He nonetheless says 'I weirdly have very little personal ambition' (2026).
claims.inference: A sustained drive to win and to hold the top role, alongside a sincere-seeming denial of personal ambition, fits Type 3: the achieving self is identified with the mission, and the image of a selfless builder is maintained. It also keeps Type 8 in contention.
claims.alternative: Ambition is required by his roles and is not type-specific. The denial may be honest: he may experience the drive as mission. 8 explains the power-seeking but not the conflict avoidance or the approval-seeking.

claims.claim: Altman's emotional disclosures (hurt, sadness, shame among other 'negative things', 'melancholy', 'nostalgic for the present', gratitude for 'bad days') appear mostly in retrospective, curated public settings: podcasts, posts, profiles, sometimes framed as going 'off-script'. Meanwhile he describes himself as not 'a high-EQ person' and as viewing subtle emotion 'with alien intrigue'. His mother says he 'keep[s] an awful lot tied up inside', and Hao reports he 'avoided expressing negative emotions' in public.
claims.inference: This is the main discriminator against the published Type 4 thesis. A core 4 tends to identify with and foreground its feelings and their nuance in real time. Altman reports low emotional attunement, brackets negative feeling in public, and names feelings after the fact in narrative form. That fits a 3 (or 3 with a 4 wing): feelings set aside for function and later narrated.
claims.alternative: The published page's vocabulary argument ('shameful', 'fugue', 'emotional depth and range') does show real emotional articulacy, especially the private Musk email (C51) and 'melancholy' (C61). A 4 with a strong 3 wing in a public CEO role could look similar. Self-reported EQ is unreliable.

claims.claim: Concern for how he will look shapes several of Altman's own choices about disclosure and framing. He withheld assault details lest he 'look like I’m manipulative or playing for sympathy' (2026). He reportedly pushed for a board statement 'absolving him of wrongdoing' (2023). He framed his equity regret around 'conspiracy theories' and what people 'seem very able to understand' (2025). He recast his Trump reversal as escaping the 'npc trap' (2025). He described himself as 'a nuanced character' under hostile questioning (2025). He blamed 'words and narratives' after the April 2026 attack.
claims.inference: Repeated attention to the public picture of himself, across topics and years, is consistent with an image-oriented (heart-triad) core. Combined with C75 and C76 it favors 3 over 4, because the attention goes to appearing credible, effective and likeable rather than distinctive or authentic.
claims.alternative: Any public figure under intense scrutiny manages perception. Some items rest on anonymous sourcing (S41). This is an interpretive pattern, not proof of motive.

claims.claim: The published page's leading thesis that Altman is Type 4 (4w3, sp/so) rests mainly on the coming-out speech, the words 'shameful' and 'fugue', the no-equity 'meaning over money' story, the Musk 'it hurts' email, 'emotional depth and range', 'I can't change my personality', and World as an identity system. Several of these supports are misquoted or unsourced: the 'heart pounding' anxiety quote, the 'skeptical of ... regulation' Senate line, 'We needed a structure that didn't exist', 'I don't know what Sam believes', and 'totally transformed'. Others are weaker than presented: 'shameful' is one word in a list; he wishes he had taken equity; he called the firing 'unfair'.
claims.inference: With the corrected record, the case for a 4 core shrinks to genuine but limited evidence: the costly adolescent disclosure, 'melancholy', and private expressions of hurt. The case against it (C19, C20, C75-C78) is repeated across decades. That is a major thesis change for a live page.
claims.alternative: A 4w3 reading remains the strongest alternative and should be argued fairly in the refreshed article, not caricatured.

claims.claim: In 'Moore's Law for Everything' (March 2021) Altman argued that 'If public policy doesn’t adapt accordingly, most people will end up worse off than they are today' and proposed sharing AI-driven wealth broadly. In 'The Intelligence Age' (September 2024) he wrote: 'I believe the future is going to be so bright that no one can do it justice by trying to write about it now'.
claims.inference: Shows a consistent public vision of abundance and techno-optimism, which recurs in his self-description ('very optimistic').
claims.alternative: Vision essays are also fundraising and policy positioning. The published page places the 'so bright' line in 'Moore's Law for Everything'; it is in 'The Intelligence Age'.

type_hypothesis.against: Real evidence resists Type 3. (1) At about 17 he chose a costly public self-disclosure, coming out to his whole school when he could have kept the speech abstract (C07). Approval-seeking does not explain that choice, though he was already 'mostly out' and it was well received. (2) He shows genuine emotional articulacy, sometimes in private: the 2023 email telling Musk 'it really fucking hurts' (C51), 'Melancholy is a better word than sad' (C61), 'chaotic and shameful and upsetting' (C36), 'nostalgic for the present' (C62), gratitude for 'bad days' and 'emotional depth and range' (C60), and meditation's 'no self' (C59). (3) He has declined or disclaimed obvious status markers: no direct OpenAI equity for a decade and $76,001 pay in 2023 (C28), '0%' excitement about being a public-company CEO and a preference for the discovery years over the public role (C29, C67), and 'very little personal ambition' (C30). He now says he wishes he had taken equity, mainly to end the questions. (4) Power and control behavior supports Type 8: 'Only if the whole board quits', 'supermad', 'Absolutely fucking not' (C37, C38), holding the line against Musk's 'unilateral control' and the 2017 'Sam stood his ground' (C41, C45), fascination with Napoleon's system 'where you can control the people' (C25), 'quick to anger' in 2016 (S03), 'I have to win, and I'm in charge of everything' (C02), and 'relentless will to power' (C40). (5) Much of the accommodation and deception testimony is anonymous, adversarial, or comes from parties to the 2023 firing (C40, C46-C49). His biographer frames it as 'a typical critique of people who have the salesman skill set' (C42). The job's incentives compete with any type explanation. (6) Conflict avoidance and wanting to be liked also fit Type 9 and Type 2. The attentiveness colleagues describe (C44) and the loyalty that produced the 745-signature letter (C34) give Type 2 some support. (7) In 2016 he claimed the 'missing circuit ... that would make me care what people think about me' is 'a real gift' (C22). That is an unusual thing for a core 3 to say, even though his 2019 statements contradict it.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 4, the published reading (4w3), remains the strongest rival. It explains the costly adolescent self-disclosure (C07) and early secrecy and difference (C06). It explains a recurring vocabulary of hurt, shame, melancholy and nostalgia (C36, C51, C61, C62), the philosophical stance that values bad experience and 'emotional depth and range' (C60), and contemplative practice and the 'no self' insight (C59). It explains his preference for the discovery years over the public CEO role and his ambivalence about equity and public markets (C28, C29, C67), and his attraction to literary and existential framings (Ozymandias, C24). A 4 with a strong 3 wing and self-preservation instinct could present as a polished, adaptive executive. Type 8 is the serious second alternative. It explains the will to power (C12, C40, C76), the hard control demands under threat (C37, C38), refusing Musk's control (C41, C45), the Napoleon fascination (C25), the survivalist streak (C26), and 'I have to win, and I'm in charge of everything' (C02). It fails the conflict test: Altman repeatedly calls himself conflict-averse (C41) and colleagues describe accommodation, not confrontation (C75). Type 2 (wanting to be liked, attentiveness used to influence, relational loyalty; C40, C44, C34) and Type 9 (conflict avoidance, 'unifying force'; C39, C41) are weaker. Neither explains the sustained drive for the top role. Type 7 (optimism, many ventures, reframing pain; C27, C60, C80) is weaker still.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What he does when keeping approval in the room conflicts with stating his own position or feeling. A core 4 typically protects the authentic expression of what it feels and believes even at the cost of approval, and foregrounds its feelings. A core 3 adapts the presented self to what wins in each room, sets feelings aside in order to function, and narrates them later. Across Loopt, YC and OpenAI (2005-2026), independent sources describe the adaptive choice: Hagey, Hao's Loopt and YC sources, Sutskever and Brockman in 2017, Sutskever's 2023 memos, a board member in 2026 (C75, C42-C46, C40). Altman names it himself repeatedly as his defining, costly flaw ('too much of a conflict avoider'; 'I am not proud of being conflict-averse, which has caused great pain'; C41, C39, C08). He twice describes himself as low in emotional attunement, in 2016 and 2025 (C19, C20). Hao reports he 'avoided expressing negative emotions' in public (C16). His feeling-disclosures are mostly retrospective and public-facing (C77), and concern for how he will look shapes his disclosures (C78). This favors 3 over 4. The same test separates 3 from 8: an 8 confronts and does not need to be liked in each interaction, while Altman confronts openly only when control of the institution is at stake (2017, 2023). The sustained drive to win and hold the top role (C76) separates 3 from 9; the achievement-and-status focus rather than being needed separates 3 from 2.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: The costly coming-out speech at 17 (C07). The private, unguarded hurt in the 2023 Musk email (C51). The persistent anxiety and melancholy strand and the meditation 'no self' insight (C59, C61). A decade without OpenAI equity, partly structural and now regretted mainly for reasons of public perception (C28). The survivalist preparation he later downplayed (C26). His 2016 claim that not caring what people think is 'a gift' (C22). How much of the accommodation pattern is a salesman's learned craft rather than core motive (C42). The wing (3w4 vs 3w2) is not settled and need not be asserted; the 4-flavored vocabulary may point to a 4 wing, the attentiveness to a 2 wing. The Annie Altman allegations (C69) are unresolved and are not type evidence in either direction.
